The Common swift (Apus apus) is an aerial insectivore renowned for its exceptional flight endurance, rarely alighting except during the breeding season. Adults of this species attain an ultimate total length of approximately 16.5 centimeters [Li = approximately 16.5 centimeters], a streamlined body plan optimized for sustained flight efficiency. The species exhibits a relatively low maximum reproductive output, reflecting its slow life-history strategy typical of long-lived birds. Field studies indicate that the maximum reproductive rate, expressed through a combination of clutch size and breeding frequency, is constrained: females typically lay two to three eggs per clutch [N_R_i = two to three eggs per clutch], but this is accompanied by only a single brood per year [F_R_i = single brood per year] under typical thermal conditions of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This annual reproductive effort, averaging fewer than three offspring per breeding season, aligns with patterns observed in other aerially-foraging Apodidae, where high adult survival and extended lifespan offset low fecundity.

At hatching, the neonatal mass of the Common swift is remarkably low. Newly emerged altricial nestlings weigh only around 2.9 grams [Wwb = around 2.9 grams], a value consistent with the extremely altricial development strategy of swifts, where chicks are born naked, blind, and completely dependent on parental provisioning at an incubation temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. This minimal birth weight stands in marked contrast to the species' ultimate adult wet weight, which reaches approximately 40.2 grams [Wwi = approximately 40.2 grams] at full somatic maturity. The nearly fourteen-fold increase from neonatal mass to asymptotic adult size underscores the rapid growth trajectory of nestlings, which must accumulate substantial reserves for flight feathers and musculature before fledging. This dramatic mass increase is supported by intensive biparental care, with adults foraging for aerial plankton throughout the day to meet the high energetic demands of their developing chicks.

The developmental chronology of the Common swift is tightly constrained by its aerial lifestyle and reliance on ephemeral insect prey. Eggs incubated at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] require an average incubation period of approximately 20.65 days [ab = approximately 20.65 days] before hatching, a duration that is intermediate among Apodidae and reflects the balance between embryonic development rates and the need to synchronize hatching with peak prey availability. Interestingly, field data compiled by Glutz von Blotzheim and Bauer (1994) indicate that this incubation period is temperature-dependent, with the 36 °C [T = 36 °C] value representing typical nest-cavity conditions during the attentive phase. The age at birth, defined here as the time from oviposition to hatching, is thus a critical parameter influencing overall breeding phenology. Shifts in ambient temperatures during the incubation period can alter this duration, potentially affecting chick condition and subsequent survival through mismatches with food abundance peaks.

Under the thermal regime typical of the active breeding season, where adult body temperatures are maintained around 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], nestling development proceeds through a series of well-defined milestones. Fledging, defined as the achievement of sustained flight and nest departure, occurs at approximately 42.5 days after hatching [tx = approximately 42.5 days after hatching] at a temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This relatively prolonged nestling period, exceeding six weeks, is necessary for the complete development of the long, narrow wings and the powerful flight musculature required for the swift's entirely aerial existence. Following fledging, juveniles enter a sub-adult phase characterized by continued refinement of flight skills and foraging efficiency. Puberty, or the attainment of sexual maturity, does not occur until considerably later: individuals typically reach reproductive maturity at roughly 127.5 days after hatching [tp = roughly 127.5 days after hatching] at a temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This delay reflects the substantial time investment needed to achieve the structural and physiological competence for breeding.

Longevity records for the Common swift illustrate a remarkable lifespan for a bird of its body size. The oldest documented individuals in the wild have been recorded living for approximately 7702 days [am = approximately 7702 days], which is equivalent to over two decades, at a typical active metabolic temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This exceptional lifespan, exceeding twenty-one years, is among the highest recorded for any passerine-size bird and is a cornerstone of the species' life-history strategy. Consistent with this extended longevity, first reproduction is notably delayed; the time since birth at the first brood averages about 730 days [tR = about 730 days] under thermal conditions of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. Individuals typically do not breed until their second or third year, investing instead in extensive somatic development and the accumulation of experience necessary for successful reproduction. This delayed onset of breeding, combined with high adult survival, exemplifies a slow-paced life history optimized for exploiting a variable aerial food resource across a long lifetime.
